nodes.name: Conformally compact Riemannian manifold
nodes.statement: We call $(M,g)$ a \emph{conformally compact Riemannian manifold} if $M$ is the interior of a compact manifold $\overline M$ with boundary $\partial\overline M=X$ and there exists a smooth function $\rho:\overline{M}\to\R_{\geq 0}$ and a Riemannian metric $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $X$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\rho|_{X}=0$; \item $d\rho\neq0$ at all points of $X$; \item $\rho^2 g$ can be extended continuously to $X$; \item $\rho^2 g|_{TX}=\gamma_{(0)}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A metric on the interior of a compact manifold admitting a defining function $\rho$ with $\rho^2g$ extending to the boundary.
differentia: $M$ is the interior of a compact manifold $\overline M$ with boundary $\partial\overline M=X$
$\rho^2 g$ can be extended continuously to $X$

nodes.name: Hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^4$ as a conformally compact metric
nodes.statement: A good example to have in mind is the hyperbolic space $\mathbb {H}^4$ consisting of the upper-half of $\R^4$ with metric \be g=\frac{dx^2+dy^2+dz^2+dt^2}{t^2}, \ee and $\rho=t$.

nodes.name: Non-uniqueness of the defining function
nodes.statement: It is important to note that the defining function $\rho$ is non-unique: for any positive function $\lambda$ on $\overline{M}$, we may consider $\tilde\rho=\lambda\rho$ which has the same properties above with $\gamma_{(0)}$ replaced by $\tilde\gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^2\gamma_{(0)}$. Therefore a conformally compact metric on $M$ only defines a conformal structure on the boundary $X=\pa \Mb$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling $\rho$ rescales $\gamma_{(0)}$, so only the boundary conformal class is well defined.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A hyperbolic metric is by definition a metric having a constant sectional curvature $-1/l^2$, where $l$ has units of length.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A conformally compact metric $g$ is called \emph{asymptotically hyperbolic} if its sectional curvature is asymptotically $-1/l^2$.

nodes.name: Characterisation of the asymptotically hyperbolic condition
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic hyperbolicity is equivalent to the boundary condition $|d\rho|^2_g=\rho^2/l^2$ on $X$.
assumptions: A conformally compact metric $g$
conclusions: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is equivalent to $|d\rho|^2_{g}=\rho^2/l^2$ at $X$

nodes.name: Conformally compact Einstein metrics are asymptotically hyperbolic
nodes.statement: We also see from this formula that conformally compact Einstein metrics, i.e.\ ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations, are automatically asymptotically hyperbolic
assumptions: conformally compact Einstein metrics, i.e.\ ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations
conclusions: are automatically asymptotically hyperbolic

nodes.name: Poincaré--Einstein metrics
nodes.statement: conformally compact Einstein metrics, i.e.\ ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations, are automatically asymptotically hyperbolic; they are called \emph{Poincar\'e--Einstein metrics}
differentia: ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations

nodes.name: Cosmological constant in terms of the hyperbolic length scale
nodes.statement: From the above formula we also get the relation between the cosmological constant appearing in the Einstein condition $R_{\mu\nu}=\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ and $l$ \be \Lambda = - \frac{3}{l^2}. \ee

nodes.name: Boundary normal form of a conformally compact metric
nodes.statement: Near the boundary $X$, we can write any conformally compact metric as \be g=\frac{l^2}{ \rho^2}\Big(\alpha d\rho^2+d\rho\otimes\beta+\beta\otimes d\rho+\gamma\Big), \ee where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are 1-parameter families of functions, 1-forms and symmetric $(2,0)$-tensors on $X$, with the following power series expansion \[ \alpha=1+\rho\alpha_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad\beta=\beta_{(0)}+\rho\beta_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots. \]
nodes.statement_short: Near-boundary expansion of a conformally compact metric in $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with power series in $\rho$.

nodes.name: Gauge reduction to $\alpha=1$, $\beta=0$
nodes.statement: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is $\alpha=1$. Furthermore, we can always achieve $\beta=0$ by an appropriate diffeomorphism: the gradient flow of $\rho$ with respect to $\rho^2 g$ identifies the level sets of $\rho$ and removes this mixed term.
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic hyperbolicity fixes $\alpha=1$, and a diffeomorphism removes the mixed term $\beta$.
assumptions: a conformally compact metric written as $g=\frac{l^2}{ \rho^2}\Big(\alpha d\rho^2+d\rho\otimes\beta+\beta\otimes d\rho+\gamma\Big)$
conclusions: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is $\alpha=1$
we can always achieve $\beta=0$ by an appropriate diffeomorphism

nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham normal form of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: In the  asymptotically hyperbolic setting, we can thus write the metric in the form: \be g=\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}d\rho^2+\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\gamma \qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots. \ee

nodes.name: Order-by-order solution of Einstein's equations in the Fefferman--Graham gauge
nodes.statement: Now, it is an exercise to write down Einstein's equations for (\ref{FG}) and solve them order by order in terms of an initially given value of $\gamma_{(0)}$. The first two terms are given by \be \gamma_{(1)}=0,\qquad \gamma_{(2)}{}_{ab}=-R_{(0)}{}_{ab}+\frac{1}{4}R_{(0)}\gamma_{(0)}{}_{ab} \ee and the third remains undetermined but constrained to satisfy $$\gamma_{(0)}^{ab}\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0,\qquad \nabla_{(0)}{}^a\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0.$$ The remaining, higher-order terms, are then recursively determined algebraically from the previous terms.
nodes.statement_short: Einstein's equations force $\gamma_{(1)}=0$, fix $\gamma_{(2)}$ by the boundary Ricci tensor, and leave $\gamma_{(3)}$ free up to trace and divergence constraints.
assumptions: Einstein's equations for (\ref{FG})
an initially given value of $\gamma_{(0)}$
conclusions: the third remains undetermined but constrained to satisfy $\gamma_{(0)}^{ab}\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0,\qquad \nabla_{(0)}{}^a\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0$
The remaining, higher-order terms, are then recursively determined algebraically from the previous terms

nodes.name: Obstruction (Fefferman--Graham)
nodes.statement: The unconstrained part of $\gamma_{(3)ab}$ is referred to as the {\it obstruction} by Fefferman-Graham.

nodes.name: Fefferman--Graham expansion
nodes.statement: We can interpret the expansion (\ref{FG}) as an instance of the initial value problem. Given the initial data on the boundary in the form of the boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$, as well as the constrained $\gamma_{(3)}$, which is best thought of as an initial momentum, we can propagate these data into the bulk, obtaining a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric, at least formally in a neighbourhood of the boundary. This is known as the \emph{Fefferman--Graham expansion}.
nodes.statement_short: Propagating boundary data $(\gamma_{(0)},\gamma_{(3)})$ into the bulk to build a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric.
nodes.genus: an instance of the initial value problem
differentia: Given the initial data on the boundary in the form of the boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$, as well as the constrained $\gamma_{(3)}$
we can propagate these data into the bulk, obtaining a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric, at least formally in a neighbourhood of the boundary

nodes.name: Expansion of the boundary volume density
nodes.statement: Using the tracelessness of $\gamma_{(3)}$, an easy calculation gives \be\nonumber \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma)} = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1+\frac{1}{2} \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(0)}^{-1} \gamma_{(2)})+ O(\rho^4) \right) = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right), \ee where we have used (\ref{gamma-2}) to get the second equality.
nodes.statement_short: The volume density expands as $\sqrt{\det\gamma_{(0)}}(1-\tfrac18\rho^2R_{(0)}+O(\rho^4))$.

nodes.name: Divergent expansion of the truncated volume $V_\epsilon$
nodes.statement: The volume of the metric (\ref{FG}), up to a surface $\rho=\epsilon$ is then \be  V_\epsilon =  l^4 \int_\epsilon \frac{d\rho}{\rho^4} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right), \ee where ${X_\epsilon}$ is the surface $\rho=\epsilon$. Thus, the volume is given by \be\nonumber V_\epsilon = \frac{l^4 }{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} - \frac{l^4 }{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} + {\rm finite\,\,\, terms}, \ee
nodes.statement_short: The cut-off volume diverges as $\epsilon^{-3}$ and $\epsilon^{-1}$ with local boundary coefficients.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume (metric setup)
nodes.statement: and the renormalised volume is then defined as \be RV:=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left(  V_\epsilon -\frac{l^4}{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} + \frac{l^4}{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} \right). \ee
nodes.statement_short: $RV$ is the $\epsilon\to0$ limit of $V_\epsilon$ after subtracting the two local boundary counter terms.

nodes.name: Conformal invariance of the renormalised volume
nodes.statement: We note that the renormalized volume is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$.
assumptions: the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$
conclusions: the renormalized volume is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$

nodes.name: Proof that the renormalised volume is conformally invariant
nodes.statement: In fact for another representative $\tilde \gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^{2}\gamma_{(0)}$, the corresponding defining function is $\tilde \rho=\lambda\rho$ for an appropriate extension of $\lambda$ from the boundary into the bulk, and $\tilde{\epsilon}=\lambda^2 \epsilon$. Then the formula (\ref{RV}) takes exactly the same form in terms of the tilded quantities, which shows that it does not matter which representative in the conformal class of the boundary is used to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the rescaled representative and observe the defining formula is form-invariant.

nodes.name: Rescale the boundary representative
nodes.statement: In fact for another representative $\tilde \gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^{2}\gamma_{(0)}$, the corresponding defining function is $\tilde \rho=\lambda\rho$ for an appropriate extension of $\lambda$ from the boundary into the bulk, and $\tilde{\epsilon}=\lambda^2 \epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the rescaled representative and the induced rescalings of $\rho$ and $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Form-invariance of the defining formula
nodes.statement: Then the formula (\ref{RV}) takes exactly the same form in terms of the tilded quantities, which shows that it does not matter which representative in the conformal class of the boundary is used to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude invariance since the formula is unchanged in tilded variables.

nodes.name: The connection action functional $S[A,M]$
nodes.statement: Let $A^i$ be an ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection on a 4-manifold $M$, and $F^i = dA^i + (1/2) \epsilon^{ijk} A^j\wedge A^k$ be its curvature 2-forms. Let $M^{ij}$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix of auxiliary fields. Let us assume for the moment that the manifold in question is compact. We will discuss the case of manifolds with boundary, relevant for this work, later. Consider the following action: \be S[A,M] = \int_M {\rm Tr}( M F\wedge F). \ee
nodes.statement_short: The gravitational action is $\int_M{\rm Tr}(MF\wedge F)$ for an ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection $A^i$ and auxiliary symmetric matrix $M^{ij}$.
differentia: $F^i = dA^i + (1/2) \epsilon^{ijk} A^j\wedge A^k$ be its curvature 2-forms
$M^{ij}$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix of auxiliary fields

nodes.name: Constraint that $M$ lies on the hypersurface $g(M)=0$
nodes.statement: We also impose a constraint on the matrix $M$, that it lie on a co-dimension one hypersurface with defining equation \be g(M)=0 \ee in the space of symmetric $3\times 3$ matrices, determined by a real valued function $g$.

nodes.name: Einstein defining function $g_{\rm E}(M)$
nodes.statement: Different hypersurfaces give different field equations; the hypersurface relevant to Einstein connections/metrics is given by \be g_{\rm E}(M) = {\rm Tr}(M^{-1}) - \Lambda, \ee where $4\Lambda$ is the scalar curvature.
nodes.genus: defining function of the codimension-one hypersurface

nodes.name: Critical points give Einstein metrics
nodes.statement: The claim is that the critical points of (\ref{action}), with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH}) give rise to Einstein metrics.
assumptions: the critical points of (\ref{action})
with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH})
conclusions: give rise to Einstein metrics

nodes.name: Connection field equation $d_A(M^{ij}F^j)=0$
nodes.statement: Varying the action (\ref{action}) with respect to the connection we get \be d_A \left( M^{ij} F^j \right) =0. \ee Here we assumed that the manifold is compact, so that the integration by parts necessary to derive this field equation is justified.

nodes.name: Matrix $X^{ij}$ of curvature wedge products
nodes.statement: To do this, we introduce an auxiliary volume form ${\mathcal V}$. We can then write \be F^i\wedge F^j = X^{ij} \,{\mathcal V}. \ee Note that a different choice of $\mathcal V$ changes the matrix $X^{ij}$ by multiplication by a function. The matrix $X$ is thus defined intrinsically only up to scale.
nodes.statement_short: $X^{ij}$ is defined by $F^i\wedge F^j=X^{ij}\mathcal V$ and is intrinsic only up to overall scale.
differentia: defined intrinsically only up to scale

nodes.name: Euler--Lagrange equation for the auxiliary matrix $M$
nodes.statement: The Euler-Lagrange equations for $M$ are then \be X = \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M}. \ee (Here, we write $\partial g/\partial M$ for the matrix defined by \[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} A^{ji} = dg\Big|_{M}(A) \] for all symmetric $A^{ij}$.)

nodes.name: Strategy: treat the field equation as a first-order PDE for $M$
nodes.statement: However, in many circumstances a more useful approach is not to solve for $M(X)$, but to interpret (\ref{eq-A}) as a first-order PDE on the matrix $M$. Solving it one can then find $X$ from (\ref{eq-M}) and thus obtain a set of first-order PDE's on the connection components. It is this strategy that will be followed below for the asymptotically hyperbolic connections.
nodes.statement_short: Rather than eliminating $M$, solve the first-order PDE for $M$ and then read off $X$ and the connection.

nodes.name: $X$ in terms of $M$ in the Einstein case
nodes.statement: Let us illustrate all this for the Einstein case (\ref{g-EH}). In this case we can rewrite (\ref{eq-M}) as $M X = - \mu M^{-1}$. Taking the trace and using the condition $g_E(M)=0$ we obtain $\mu$. Thus, all in all for the Einstein case \be X = \frac{1}{\Lambda} {\rm Tr}(M X) M^{-2}, \ee which gives $X$ in terms of $M$, up to scale. (We can do no better, since $X$ is only defined up to scale, which was fixed by our choice of $\mathcal V$.)
nodes.statement_short: In the Einstein case $X=\Lambda^{-1}{\rm Tr}(MX)M^{-2}$, determining $X$ from $M$ up to scale.

nodes.name: Conformal metric defined by self-duality of the curvature 2-forms
nodes.statement: First, one constructs the conformal metric. This is the unique conformal structure that makes the triple of curvature 2-forms $F^i$ self-dual. Explicitly, \be \sqrt{{\rm det(g)}} \, g_{\mu\nu} \sim \tilde{\epsilon}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \epsilon^{ijk} F^i_{\mu\alpha} F^j_{\nu\beta} F^k_{\gamma\delta}. \ee (Note this requires a non-degeneracy condition on the $F^i$, that the matrix $X^{ij}$ above in equation (\ref{X}) be definite.)
nodes.statement_short: The conformal metric is the unique one making the curvature 2-forms $F^i$ self-dual.
nodes.origin_citation: Fine, Krasnov & Panov 2014; Herfray, Krasnov & Shtanov 2015
differentia: the unique conformal structure that makes the triple of curvature 2-forms $F^i$ self-dual

nodes.name: Volume form fixed by ${\rm Tr}(MF\wedge F)$
nodes.statement: Second, one fixes the volume form ${\mathcal V}_g$ of the metric to be \be - 2\Lambda \, {\mathcal V}_g = {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F). \ee With this choice of volume form, the action (\ref{action}) has the geometric interpretation of the total volume, up to overall scale.  The numerical factor in this formula is adjusted to agree with some conventions introduced later.
nodes.statement_short: The metric's volume form is fixed by $-2\Lambda\,\mathcal V_g={\rm Tr}(MF\wedge F)$, making the action the total volume.

nodes.name: Metric of a solution of the Euler--Lagrange equations is Einstein
nodes.statement: When the connection satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equations (\ref{eq-A}), (\ref{eq-M-gr}), the corresponding metric will be Einstein (see \cite{Herfray:2015fpa} for the proof).
assumptions: the connection satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equations (\ref{eq-A}), (\ref{eq-M-gr})
conclusions: the corresponding metric will be Einstein

nodes.name: Instanton defining function gives self-dual General Relativity
nodes.statement: Repacing $M$ by $M^{-1}$ in this function, setting $g_{inst}={\rm Tr}(M) - \Lambda$, turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics, see \cite{Herfray:2015fpa} for a discussion of this.
assumptions: Repacing $M$ by $M^{-1}$ in this function, setting $g_{inst}={\rm Tr}(M) - \Lambda$
conclusions: turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics

nodes.name: Modified defining function $g_{mod}(M)={\rm det}(M)-\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Another very interesting modification that can be considered is to set \be g_{mod}(M) = {\rm det}(M) - \Lambda. \ee This gives a theory in many ways simpler than GR. In fact, this is the theory that was studied by one of us in \cite{Joel}, albeit in its``pure connection'' version without the matrix $M$.
nodes.genus: defining function of the constraint hypersurface

nodes.name: All results hold for an arbitrary defining function $g(M)$
nodes.statement: Details of these modified theories will not be important for us here, because we will be solving the arising equations in general for an arbitrary function $g(M)$. All our results below apply equally to the modified theories as well as to GR. In the deformed case, one continues to define the metric by the condition that the curvature 2-forms are self-dual. The volume form is then fixed to be a constant multiple of the form ${\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F)$, so that the action (\ref{action}) continues to receive the interpretation of the total volume of the space.
nodes.statement_short: The analysis is carried out for arbitrary $g(M)$, so it covers GR and all deformed theories alike.

nodes.name: Self-dual ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: We may now express the $SU(2)$-connection $A^i$ in terms of the 1-parameter families of (co-)frames and spin connections on $X$ as \be A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+{}^\gamma\omega^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}\gamma(\dot e^j,e^k)d\rho, \ee where ${}^\gamma\omega^i=-(1/2)\epsilon^{ijk}\, {}^\gamma\omega^{jk}$.
nodes.statement_short: The self-dual part of the Levi-Civita connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric has a simple first-order pole in $\rho$ plus boundary spin-connection terms.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
assumptions: Given an asymptotically hyperbolic 4-manifold $(M,g)$
$e^i$ denotes a 1-parameter family of local coframes for the 1-parameter family of metrics $\gamma$ on $X$
conclusions: $A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+{}^\gamma\omega^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}\gamma(\dot e^j,e^k)d\rho$

nodes.name: Computation of the self-dual Levi-Civita connection
nodes.statement: Given an asymptotically hyperbolic 4-manifold $(M,g)$, we now compute the Levi-Civita connection on the bundle of self-dual 2-forms. First we choose a local coframe for $g$ adapted to the chosen conformal compactification $$\theta^i=\frac{l}{\rho}e^i,\qquad\theta^4=\frac{l}{\rho}d\rho,$$ where $e^i$ denotes a 1-parameter family of local coframes for the 1-parameter family of metrics $\gamma$ on $X$. The spin connection is then computed by decomposing the structure equation as $$\begin{cases}d\theta^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge \theta^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge \theta^4=0 \cr d\theta^4+\omega^4{}_i\wedge \theta^i=0, \end{cases}$$ or, equivalently $$\begin{cases} de^i-\frac{1}{\rho}d\rho\wedge e^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge e^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge d\rho=0 \cr \omega^4{}_i\wedge e^i=0.\end{cases}$$ These equations can be readily solved in terms of the (co-)triad $e^i$ and the associated $\gamma$-compatible spin connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j$ $$\begin{cases} \omega^i{}_j={}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)-\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)d\rho \cr \omega^{4i}=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j. \end{cases}$$ Here dot denotes the derivative with respect to $\rho$, and $\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)$ is the metric product of 1-forms $\dot e^i$ and $e^j$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose an adapted coframe, decompose Cartan's structure equations, and solve them for the spin connection.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Choose an adapted coframe
nodes.statement: First we choose a local coframe for $g$ adapted to the chosen conformal compactification $$\theta^i=\frac{l}{\rho}e^i,\qquad\theta^4=\frac{l}{\rho}d\rho,$$ where $e^i$ denotes a 1-parameter family of local coframes for the 1-parameter family of metrics $\gamma$ on $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the coframe $\theta^i=(l/\rho)e^i$, $\theta^4=(l/\rho)d\rho$ adapted to the compactification.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Decompose the structure equation
nodes.statement: The spin connection is then computed by decomposing the structure equation as $$\begin{cases}d\theta^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge \theta^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge \theta^4=0 \cr d\theta^4+\omega^4{}_i\wedge \theta^i=0, \end{cases}$$ or, equivalently $$\begin{cases} de^i-\frac{1}{\rho}d\rho\wedge e^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge e^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge d\rho=0 \cr \omega^4{}_i\wedge e^i=0.\end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Split Cartan's first structure equation into tangential and radial parts.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Solve for the spin connection
nodes.statement: These equations can be readily solved in terms of the (co-)triad $e^i$ and the associated $\gamma$-compatible spin connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j$ $$\begin{cases} \omega^i{}_j={}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)-\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)d\rho \cr \omega^{4i}=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Read off $\omega^i{}_j$ and $\omega^{4i}$ in terms of the boundary triad and its $\rho$-derivative.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Leading-order contribution for Einstein asymptotically hyperbolic metrics
nodes.statement: Let us note that for an asymptotically hyperbolic metric that is also Einstein, equation (\ref{gamma-2}) is satisfied. The first of these conditions then implies that the third term in (\ref{A-metric}) starts with a term $O(\rho)$, so that the connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i$ compatible with $e^i$ is the only contribution at order $O(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: For Einstein metrics $\gamma_{(1)}=0$, so the boundary Levi-Civita connection is the only $O(1)$ term.
nodes.section: SO(3)-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Bundle setup: $P|_X$ isomorphic to the frame bundle of $X$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the interior of a compact manifold $\overline{M}$ with boundary $\partial\overline M=X$. Let $P\to\overline M$ be an ${\rm SO}(3)$ or ${\rm SU}(2)$-bundle over $\overline M$ and denote by $P|_M\to M$ its restriction to $M$ and by $P|_X\to X$ its restriction to $X$. We require $P|_X$ to be abstractly isomorphic to the frame bundle of $X$.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection
nodes.statement: We shall call an ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection $A^i$ on $P|_M$ \emph{asymptotically hyperbolic} if there exists a smooth function $\rho:\overline{M}\to\R_+$ and a smooth connection $\omega$ on $P$ defined on the whole of $\overline{M}$, such that \begin{itemize} \item $\rho$ is a boundary defining function, i.e., $\rho|_{X}=0$ and $d\rho|_{X}\neq0$; \item The endomorphism-valued 1-form $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)$ extends smoothly to $X$; \item The restriction $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)|_{TX}=e^i_{(0)}$ is a coframing for $X$. Equivalently, $\rho(A-\omega)|_{TX} \in T^*X \otimes \mathfrak(P|_X)$ gives an isomorphism $TX \to \mathfrak{su}(P|_X)$. \end{itemize} The last condition here should is the analogue of the condition that a conformally compact metric $g$ should have $\rho^2g|_X$ a metric on $X$.
nodes.statement_short: A connection is asymptotically hyperbolic when $\rho(A-\omega)$ extends smoothly to the boundary and restricts there to a coframing.
differentia: $\rho$ is a boundary defining function, i.e., $\rho|_{X}=0$ and $d\rho|_{X}\neq0$
The restriction $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)|_{TX}=e^i_{(0)}$ is a coframing for $X$

nodes.name: Independence of choices and the induced boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$
nodes.statement: It is immediate that the definition does not depend on the choices of $\rho$ or $\omega$. Given an asymptotically hyperbolic connection, we can define a metric $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $X$ by declaring $e^i_{(0)}$to be an orthonormal coframe. This fixes an isomorphism $P|_X \to TX$. It is then convenient to take $\omega^i$ to be an arbitrary extension of the Levi-Civita connection $\omega_{(0)}^i$ of $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $P|_X$ to the whole of $P \to \overline{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: The definition is independent of $\rho$ and $\omega$, and an asymptotically hyperbolic connection canonically induces a boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$.
assumptions: Given an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
conclusions: the definition does not depend on the choices of $\rho$ or $\omega$
we can define a metric $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $X$ by declaring $e^i_{(0)}$to be an orthonormal coframe
This fixes an isomorphism $P|_X \to TX$

nodes.name: General form of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement: Thus, in general, an asymptotically hyperbolic ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection may be written as: \be A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i_{(0)}+\omega^i_{(0)}+a^i+b^id\rho \ee where \[ a^i=a^i_{(0)}+\rho a^i_{(1)}+\cdots, \qquad b^i=b^i_{(0)}+\rho b^i_{(1)}+\cdots \] are 1-parameter families of 1-forms and functions on $X$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: An asymptotically hyperbolic connection is a first-order pole $e^i_{(0)}/\rho$ plus the boundary Levi-Civita connection plus regular terms.

nodes.name: Curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement: The curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is: \be F^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\Si^i_{(0)}+\Oc (1) = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\left( d\rho\W e^i_{(0)}-\frac{\eps^{ijk}}{2}e^j_{(0)}\W e^k_{(0)} \right )+\Oc (1). \ee Note that there is no $1/\rho$ term here because $d_{\omega_{(0)}} e_{(0)}^i = 0$ (since $\omega_{(0)}$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_{(0)}$).
nodes.statement_short: The curvature has a double pole whose leading coefficient is the boundary self-dual 2-form $\Sigma^i_{(0)}$, with no $1/\rho$ term.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: The metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is asymptotically hyperbolic
nodes.statement: From (\ref{volume}), remembering $\Lambda=-3/l^2$, we immediately get that the metric defined by the connection, asymptotically, is \be \frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\Oc (1), \ee which is an asymptotically hyperbolic metric of sectional curvature $-1/l^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The metric algebraically built from an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is itself asymptotically hyperbolic with curvature $-1/l^2$.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
assumptions: From (\ref{volume}), remembering $\Lambda=-3/l^2$
conclusions: the metric defined by the connection, asymptotically, is $\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\Oc (1)$
which is an asymptotically hyperbolic metric of sectional curvature $-1/l^2$

nodes.name: Two-step computation of the metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement: The metric is computed in two steps. First, we need to find a metric that makes the curvature 2-forms self-dual. The curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is: \be F^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\Si^i_{(0)}+\Oc (1) = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\left( d\rho\W e^i_{(0)}-\frac{\eps^{ijk}}{2}e^j_{(0)}\W e^k_{(0)} \right )+\Oc (1). \ee Note that there is no $1/\rho$ term here because $d_{\omega_{(0)}} e_{(0)}^i = 0$ (since $\omega_{(0)}$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_{(0)}$). The conformal metric in which these 2-forms are self-dual is a multiple of \[ \frac{1}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\Oc (1). \] As is clear from (\ref{curv-asympt}), asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$. From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$. This in particular implies that the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) is automatically satisfied, as it reduces to the Bianchi identity for the curvature. Thus, asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations. To fix the metric, we compute, asymptotically \be {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = \frac{3}{\Lambda}{\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} \frac{6}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge e_{(0)}^1\wedge e_{(0)}^2\wedge e_{(0)}^3. \ee
nodes.statement_short: First fix the conformal class by self-duality of $F^i$, then fix the scale using ${\rm Tr}(MF\wedge F)$.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: Fix the conformal class by self-duality
nodes.statement: First, we need to find a metric that makes the curvature 2-forms self-dual. The curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is: \be F^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\Si^i_{(0)}+\Oc (1) = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\left( d\rho\W e^i_{(0)}-\frac{\eps^{ijk}}{2}e^j_{(0)}\W e^k_{(0)} \right )+\Oc (1). \ee Note that there is no $1/\rho$ term here because $d_{\omega_{(0)}} e_{(0)}^i = 0$ (since $\omega_{(0)}$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_{(0)}$). The conformal metric in which these 2-forms are self-dual is a multiple of \[ \frac{1}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\Oc (1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute the curvature and identify the conformal class in which it is self-dual.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: Fix the volume form to fix the metric
nodes.statement: To fix the metric, we compute, asymptotically \be {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = \frac{3}{\Lambda}{\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} \frac{6}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge e_{(0)}^1\wedge e_{(0)}^2\wedge e_{(0)}^3. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate ${\rm Tr}(MF\wedge F)$ asymptotically to pin down the volume form and hence the metric.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic connections automatically solve the field equations asymptotically
nodes.statement: As is clear from (\ref{curv-asympt}), asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$. From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$. This in particular implies that the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) is automatically satisfied, as it reduces to the Bianchi identity for the curvature. Thus, asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations.
nodes.statement_short: Since $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$ forces $M^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$, the field equation reduces to the Bianchi identity and holds automatically.

assumptions: asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$
From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$
