nodes.name: First-order pole versus second-order pole
nodes.statement: As we have already emphasised in the Introduction, one of the main differences between the metric and connection setups is that in the later case the requirement (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) of a first-order pole in the radial coordinate automatically gives rise to connections asymptotically satisfying the field equations. This should be contrasted to the metric case, where the requirement (\ref{FG}) of a second-order pole only gives the conformal compactness condition and an extra condition must be imposed to obtain asymptotically hyperbolic metrics.
nodes.statement_short: In the connection setting conformal compactness and asymptotic hyperbolicity cannot be separated, unlike in the metric setting.
nodes.section: Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: Boundary term in the variation of the action
nodes.statement: The variation of ${\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F)$ produces a boundary term \be \delta \int {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = 2 \int_X {\rm Tr}( M F \wedge \delta A) + \ldots, \ee where the dots stand for terms proportional to field equations.

nodes.name: Boundary condition: $M$ asymptotically a multiple of the identity
nodes.statement: A convenient choice of boundary conditions for the variational principle is then as follows. Instead of fixing the connection on the boundary, which is inconvenient because the connection has a first order pole there, we can require that asymptotically and to a sufficiently high order in the radial coordinate expansion (see below) the matrix of auxiliary fields is a multiple of the identity matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Impose boundary conditions on $M$ (asymptotically proportional to the identity) rather than on the singular connection.

nodes.name: Chern--Simons invariant $S^{CS}_X[A]$
nodes.statement: Then the boundary term (\ref{b-term}) arising in the variation of the action is cancelled by the Chern--Simons invariant of the restriction of the connection to the boundary \be S^{CS}_X[A] = \int_X \left( A^i \wedge dA^i + \frac{1}{3} \epsilon^{ijk} A^i\wedge A^j\wedge A^k\right), \ee which has the property \be \delta S^{CS}_X[A] = 2 \int_X {\rm Tr}(F \wedge \delta A). \ee
nodes.statement_short: The boundary Chern--Simons functional of the restricted connection, whose variation reproduces $2\int_X{\rm Tr}(F\wedge\delta A)$.
nodes.genus: Chern--Simons invariant of the restriction of the connection to the boundary

nodes.name: The required boundary term is the boundary Chern--Simons invariant
nodes.statement: Thus, with the boundary condition being those on $M$, the required boundary term is just the Chern--Simons invariant of the boundary connection. Below we shall see that this is also a good choice for cancelling the divergent contributions coming from the bulk part of the action, once everything is evaluated on a solution to field equations.
nodes.statement_short: With boundary conditions imposed on $M$, well-posedness of the variational principle requires exactly the boundary Chern--Simons term.
assumptions: with the boundary condition being those on $M$
conclusions: the required boundary term is just the Chern--Simons invariant of the boundary connection

nodes.name: Solve the connection field equations order by order in the radial coordinate
nodes.statement: In this section we solve the field equations (\ref{eq-A}) and (\ref{eq-M}) by expanding the fields in a power series in the radial coordinate. We start by discussing the 3+1 decomposition of the connection field equations.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the connection field equations as a radial power series -- the connection analogue of the Fefferman--Graham problem.

nodes.name: 3+1 decomposition of the connection and its curvature
nodes.statement: We fix a boundary defining function $\rho\in C^\infty(M,\R_{\geq 0})$ and decompose the connection $A^i$ as $$A^i=\alpha^i+\beta^id\rho$$ where $\alpha^i$ and $\beta^i$ are 1-parameter families of 1-forms and functions on $X$. The curvature of $A$ is then $$F_A^i=f_\alpha^i-(\dot\alpha^i-d^X_\alpha\beta^i)\wedge d\rho,$$ where $d^X_\alpha$ is the covariant exterior derivative with respect to connection $\alpha^i$ along the hypersurface $\rho=\text{const}$, and $f^i_\alpha$ is the curvature of $\alpha^i$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $A^i$ into tangential $\alpha^i$ and radial $\beta^i$ parts and decompose the curvature accordingly.

nodes.name: Momentum $\pi^i$ conjugate to $\alpha^i$
nodes.statement: Defining the momentum $\pi^i$ canonically conjugate to $\alpha^i$ by \be \pi^i = M^{ij} f^j_\alpha, \ee

nodes.name: 3+1 form of the connection field equations
nodes.statement: the 3+1 decomposition of the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) reads \be \begin{cases} \dot\pi^i+[\beta,\pi]^i=d^X_\alpha\Big(M^{ij}(\dot\alpha^j-d^X_\alpha\beta^j)\Big), \cr d^X_\alpha \pi^i=0. \end{cases} \ee
nodes.statement_short: An evolution equation for $\pi^i$ together with the Gauss-type constraint $d^X_\alpha\pi^i=0$.

nodes.name: Only three constraint equations in the connection formulation
nodes.statement: The first set of equations can be viewed as evolution equations for the momentum 2-forms $\pi^i$. However, it is better to think of them as first-order evolution equations for the matrix $M^{ij}$. The matrix $M^{ij}$ then determines $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), which in turn determines the evolution of $\alpha^i$ via (\ref{X-alpha}). The second set of equations are the constraints that the matrix $M^{ij}$ should satisfy, relating $M^{ij}$ to $X^{ij}$. One of the important features of the connection formulation is that there are only 3 constraint equations to be satisfied, to be compared with 4 diffeomorphism constraints in the metric approach. We further discuss the evolution equations (\ref{feqs}) from the Hamiltonian viewpoint in the Appendix.
nodes.statement_short: Read the evolution equations as first-order equations for $M^{ij}$; the connection setting has only 3 constraints versus 4 in the metric setting.

nodes.name: Partial gauge fixing $\beta^i=0$ (temporal gauge)
nodes.statement: For now, we just fix a part of the gauge freedom, by setting $\beta^i=0$. This can always be done by e.g. an ${\rm SO}(3)$ gauge transformation. (Geometrically, one uses parallel transport in the radial directions to identify the restrictions of $P$ to the hypersurfaces $\rho = \text{const}$ and in this gauge $\beta^i=0$; this is sometimes called ``temporal gauge'' when treating the equations as an initial value problem.)  We then write the $\alpha^i$ part of the connection in the form $$\alpha^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$ with $$ e^i = e^i_{(0)} + \rho \, e^i_{(1)} + \ldots,$$ and $\omega_{(0)}$ being the Levi-Civita connection of the frame $e_{(0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\beta^i=0$ by an ${\rm SO}(3)$ gauge transformation and expand $\alpha^i=e^i/\rho+\omega^i_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: The gauge $\beta^i=0$ is incompatible with the metric Fefferman--Graham gauge
nodes.statement: Note that the gauge-fixing condition $\beta^i=0$ is not compatible with the gauge used in the metric setting, see (\ref{FG}). Indeed, as we have previously computed, the connection corresponding to metric (\ref{FG}) is of the form (\ref{A-metric}), and in particular has a $d\rho$ term. The gauge $\beta^i=0$, quite convenient in calculations, will thus fail to produce a metric in the gauge (\ref{FG}). This just means that the most natural coordinate systems used in the metric and connection settings are different.
nodes.statement_short: Temporal gauge and the Fefferman--Graham metric gauge are different natural coordinate choices.

nodes.name: Radial derivative and spatial curvature of $\alpha^i$
nodes.statement: The derivative of the $\alpha^i$ with respect to the radial coordinate, denoted by the dot, is \be \dot{\alpha}^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2} e^i + \frac{1}{\rho} \dot{e}^i. \ee The spatial curvature of $\alpha$ is given by \be f_\alpha^i=\frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}e^j\wedge e^k+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^i+f^i_{(0)}, \ee where $D\equiv d^X_{\omega_{(0)}}$ is the covariant derivative along the boundary $X$ with respect to $\omega_{(0)}$ and $f^i_{(0)}: = d\omega_{(0)}^i + (1/2)\epsilon^{ijk} \omega_{(0)}^j\omega_{(0)}^k$ is the curvature of $\omega_{(0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $\rho$-expansions of $\dot\alpha^i$ and of the spatial curvature $f^i_\alpha$ in the gauge $\beta^i=0$.

nodes.name: Matrix $X^{ij}$ relative to the reference volume form $\mathcal V_0$
nodes.statement: We now define the matrix $X^{ij}$ via \be f_\alpha^{(i}\wedge \dot{\alpha}^{j)} = X^{ij}\, {\mathcal V}_0, \qquad {\mathcal V}_0 = \frac{1}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge \frac{1}{6}\epsilon^{ijk} e^i_{(0)}\wedge e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: $X^{ij}$ is normalised against the reference volume form $\mathcal V_0=\rho^{-4}d\rho\wedge dv_0$.
nodes.genus: matrix of curvature wedge products relative to $\mathcal V_0$

nodes.name: Expansion of $X^{ij}$ starts with the identity matrix
nodes.statement: The reason for choosing this volume form to define $X^{ij}$ is that its expansion in powers of $\rho$ starts with the identity matrix \be X^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho X^{ij}_{(1)} +\ldots. \ee We will compute terms in this expansion below.
assumptions: choosing this volume form to define $X^{ij}$
conclusions: its expansion in powers of $\rho$ starts with the identity matrix
$X^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho X^{ij}_{(1)} +\ldots$

nodes.name: The auxiliary matrix $M$ is a multiple of the identity to leading order
nodes.statement: The fact that the expansion for $X^{ij}$ starts with the identity implies that also the matrix $M^{ij}$, which is algebraically expressed in terms of $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), to leading order is a multiple of the identity matrix. For example, for the Einstein case we have \be \frac{\Lambda}{3} M = \sum_n (-1)^n \left( \frac{3\Psi}{\Lambda}\right)^n, \ee where $\Psi$ is a trace free matrix whose expansion starts with order $\rho$ (or higher). So, we write \be M \sim m^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho m^{ij}_{(1)} + \ldots, \ee  for an appropriate multiple of $M$. This expansion can then be used in field equations (\ref{feqs}).
nodes.statement_short: Because $X^{ij}=\delta^{ij}+O(\rho)$, an appropriate multiple $m^{ij}$ of $M^{ij}$ also expands as $\delta^{ij}+O(\rho)$.
assumptions: The fact that the expansion for $X^{ij}$ starts with the identity
the matrix $M^{ij}$, which is algebraically expressed in terms of $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M})
conclusions: to leading order is a multiple of the identity matrix
$M \sim m^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho m^{ij}_{(1)} + \ldots$

nodes.name: Evolution equation for the matrix $m^{ij}$
nodes.statement: We can now write down the first of the equations in (\ref{feqs}) as an equation on the matrix $m\sim M$, where for a general theory an appropriate multiple of $M$ is taken so that the expansion for $m$ starts with the identity matrix. After some cancelations and rewriting, the equation reads \be \dot{m}^{ij} \left( \frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k\wedge e^l+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^j+f^j_{(0)}\right) = (Dm^{ij})\wedge \left( -\frac{1}{\rho^2} e^i + \frac{1}{\rho} \dot{e}^i\right) \\ \nonumber + \frac{1}{\rho} (\epsilon^{ikj} m^{jl} - m^{ij} \epsilon^{jkl}) e^k  \wedge \left( -\frac{1}{\rho^2} e^l + \frac{1}{\rho} \dot{e}^l\right). \ee
nodes.statement_short: The first field equation written as a first-order radial evolution equation for $m^{ij}$.

nodes.name: Cancellation of the $1/\rho^3$ term forces the identity leading order
nodes.statement: The left-had-side starts with terms of the order $1/\rho^2$, while there is a term of order $1/\rho^3$ on the right. This term cancels only when the expansion of $m$ starts with a multiple of the identity matrix. So, this equation once again tells us (\ref{m-exp}) should hold.
nodes.statement_short: Consistency of the leading powers of $\rho$ in the evolution equation independently forces $m=\mathbb{I}+O(\rho)$.
assumptions: The left-had-side starts with terms of the order $1/\rho^2$, while there is a term of order $1/\rho^3$ on the right
conclusions: This term cancels only when the expansion of $m$ starts with a multiple of the identity matrix
this equation once again tells us (\ref{m-exp}) should hold

nodes.name: $m_{(1)}=0$
nodes.statement: We get an equation for $m_{(1)}$ by keeping terms of order $1/\rho^2$ on both sides. We get \be \dot{m}^{ij} \frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)} + (\epsilon^{ikj} m^{jl}_{(1)} - m^{ij}_{(1)} \epsilon^{jkl}) e^k_{(0)}  \wedge e^l_{(0)} =0. \ee We now use \be e^i\wedge e^j = \epsilon^{ijk} \frac{1}{2} \epsilon^{klm} e^l\wedge e^m \ee to get \be 0=m^{ij}_{(1)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(1)} - m^{in}_{(1)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - 2m^{ij}_{(1)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(1)}), \ee which implies that \be m_{(1)}=0. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Matching the $1/\rho^2$ terms in the evolution equation gives an algebraic identity forcing $m_{(1)}=0$.
assumptions: keeping terms of order $1/\rho^2$ on both sides
conclusions: $0=m^{ij}_{(1)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(1)} - m^{in}_{(1)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - 2m^{ij}_{(1)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(1)})$

nodes.name: $m_{(2)}=0$
nodes.statement: We get $m_{(2)}$ by exactly the same logic, keeping terms of order $1/\rho$ on both sides. We get \be 0=2m^{ij}_{(2)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(2)} - m^{in}_{(2)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - m^{ij}_{(2)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(2)}), \ee which implies that \be m_{(2)}=0. \ee
nodes.statement_short: The same matching at order $1/\rho$ gives $m_{(2)}=0$.
assumptions: keeping terms of order $1/\rho$ on both sides
conclusions: $0=2m^{ij}_{(2)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(2)} - m^{in}_{(2)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - m^{ij}_{(2)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(2)})$

nodes.name: Only the trace of $m_{(3)}$ is constrained; its trace-free part is free
nodes.statement: The new phenomenon appears at the next order, where we keep $O(1)$ terms. We now get \be 0=3m^{ij}_{(3)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(3)} - m^{in}_{(3)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}=  \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(3)}). \ee So, in this case the evolution equation only constraints the trace part of $m_{(3)}$ to vanish. Its trace free part remains arbitrary.
nodes.statement_short: At order $\rho^3$ the evolution equation only kills ${\rm Tr}(m_{(3)})$, leaving the trace-free part free -- the connection analogue of the Fefferman--Graham obstruction.
assumptions: we keep $O(1)$ terms
conclusions: $0=3m^{ij}_{(3)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(3)} - m^{in}_{(3)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}=  \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(3)})$
the evolution equation only constraints the trace part of $m_{(3)}$ to vanish
Its trace free part remains arbitrary

nodes.name: The constraint equation in expanded form
nodes.statement: The second constraint equation in (\ref{feqs}) takes the form \be D\left( m^{ij} \left( \frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k\wedge e^l+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^j+f^j_{(0)} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \epsilon^{ijk} e^j \wedge m^{kn} \left( \frac{1}{\rho}D e^n+f^n_{(0)}\right) =0. \ee We dropped one of the terms inside the second pair of brackets here, because it is easy to see that it is proportional to $\epsilon^{ijk} m^{jk}$, which is zero in view of the symmetry of $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit radial form of the Gauss constraint $d^X_\alpha\pi^i=0$.

nodes.name: Transversality condition on $m_{(3)}$
nodes.statement: As we already know from the considerations above, the expansion for $m$, after the leading identity matrix term, continues with a term of order $\rho^3$, which is trace free. Then the leading order term in (\ref{constraint}) is \be (Dm^{ij}_{(3)})\wedge \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}=0, \ee which gives a further restriction on the matrix $m$.
nodes.statement_short: The constraint equation imposes a transversality (divergence-free) condition on the free trace-free $m_{(3)}$.
assumptions: the expansion for $m$, after the leading identity matrix term, continues with a term of order $\rho^3$, which is trace free
conclusions: the leading order term in (\ref{constraint}) is $(Dm^{ij}_{(3)})\wedge \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}=0$
which gives a further restriction on the matrix $m$

nodes.name: Trace-free parts of $X_{(1)}$ and $X_{(2)}$ vanish
nodes.statement: From the fact that the matrix $m\sim M$ has an expansion of the form $m = \id + \rho^3 m_{(3)}+\ldots$, together with the fact that $X$ is algebraically determined by $M$ up to scale, see (\ref{eq-M}), we can immediately deduce that in (\ref{X-exp}) \be X_{(1)}^{ij}\Big|_{tf}= X_{(2)}^{ij}\Big|_{tf}=0. \ee We can only conclude that the trace free parts vanish, because the trace part of $X$ is not constrained by the equation (\ref{eq-M}) (indeed $X$ only makes invariant sense up to overall scale).
nodes.statement_short: Since $m=\mathbb{I}+O(\rho^3)$ and $X$ is algebraically fixed by $M$ up to scale, the trace-free parts of $X_{(1)}$ and $X_{(2)}$ vanish.
assumptions: the matrix $m\sim M$ has an expansion of the form $m = \id + \rho^3 m_{(3)}+\ldots$
the fact that $X$ is algebraically determined by $M$ up to scale, see (\ref{eq-M})
conclusions: We can only conclude that the trace free parts vanish, because the trace part of $X$ is not constrained by the equation (\ref{eq-M})

nodes.name: $X_{(1)}$ in terms of the frame coefficient $\gamma_{(1)}$
nodes.statement: Let us now compute $X_{(1)}^{ij}$ in terms of the connection. To this end, it is convenient to write \be e^i = \gamma^{ij} e^j_{(0)}. \ee The matrix $X$ is given by \be X^{ij} \frac{1}{6}\epsilon^{ijk} e^i_{(0)}\wedge e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)} = \left( \frac{1}{2} \epsilon^{(i|kl} e^k\wedge e^l + \rho D e^{(i} + \rho^2 f^{(i}_{(0)}\right) \wedge \left( e^{j)} - \rho \dot{e}^{j)}\right). \ee A simple computation gives \be X^{ij}_{(1)} = \epsilon^{(i|kl} \gamma^{kn}_{(1)} \epsilon^{nl|j)} = \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(1)}) - \gamma_{(1)}^{(ij)}. \ee It is clear that we can only conclude from (\ref{X-12}) that the trace free part of $\gamma_{(1)}$ vanishes. To determine all of it we need to do more gauge-fixing.
nodes.statement_short: Writing $e^i=\gamma^{ij}e^j_{(0)}$ gives $X^{ij}_{(1)}=\delta^{ij}{\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(1)})-\gamma_{(1)}^{(ij)}$.

nodes.name: Complete gauge fixing: $\gamma$ symmetric with trace-free higher orders
nodes.statement: We fix the gauge completely. Thus, we require that $\gamma$ be symmetric and, also, that all terms except $\gamma_{(0)}=\id$ be trace free \be \gamma^{ij}=\gamma^{(ij)}, \qquad {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(n)})=0, \quad n>1. \ee The fact that this gauge condition, together with the imposed earlier $\beta^i=0$ is an admissible gauge, is demonstrated in the Appendix.
nodes.statement_short: Complete the gauge fixing by requiring $\gamma$ symmetric and all subleading orders trace free.

nodes.name: $\gamma_{(1)}=0$
nodes.statement: Having fixed the gauge, the equation (\ref{X-12}) with (\ref{eq-gamma-1}) fix \be \gamma_{(1)}^{ij}=0. \ee
assumptions: Having fixed the gauge
the equation (\ref{X-12}) with (\ref{eq-gamma-1})

nodes.name: $\gamma_{(2)}$ determined by the boundary curvature
nodes.statement: Taking (\ref{gamma-1}) into account, it is easy to compute $X_{(2)}$. Taking into account the gauge-fixing conditions (\ref{gauge}) we get \be X_{(2)}^{ij} = - 2\gamma_{(2)}^{ij} + f^{ij}_{(0)}, \ee where we introduced the components of the curvature \be f^i_{(0)} = \frac{1}{2} f^{ij}_{(0)} \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}. \ee The matrix $f^{ij}_{(0)}$ is related to the Ricci curvature, see below, and is hence symmetric. From (\ref{X-12}) we get \be \gamma_{(2)}^{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( f^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} {\rm Tr}(f_{(0)}) \delta^{ij}\right). \ee
nodes.statement_short: The second-order frame coefficient is the trace-free part of the boundary curvature matrix, $\gamma_{(2)}=\tfrac12(f_{(0)}-\tfrac13{\rm Tr}(f_{(0)})\delta)$.
assumptions: Taking (\ref{gamma-1}) into account
Taking into account the gauge-fixing conditions (\ref{gauge})
From (\ref{X-12})
conclusions: $\gamma_{(2)}^{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( f^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} {\rm Tr}(f_{(0)}) \delta^{ij}\right)$

nodes.name: Boundary Riemann and Ricci curvature in terms of $f^{ij}_{(0)}$
nodes.statement: Now, from (\ref{f-ij}) the Riemann curvature of the zeroth order metric is given by \be R^{ij \, mn}_{(0)} = \epsilon^{ikj}  f^{kl}_{(0)} \epsilon^{lmn}. \ee Hence the Ricci tensor is \be R_{(0)\,ij} = R_{(0)\,imj}{}^m = f_{(0)\,ij} - \delta_{ij} {\rm Tr}(f_{(0)}). \ee or equivalently \be f^{ij}_{(0)} = R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{2} \delta^{ij} R_{(0)}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: $f^{ij}_{(0)}$ is the boundary Einstein tensor $R^{ij}_{(0)}-\tfrac12\delta^{ij}R_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: $\gamma_{(2)}$ in terms of the boundary Ricci tensor
nodes.statement: Hence, we can equivalently write $\gamma_{(2)}$ as \be \gamma_{(2)}^{ij} =\frac{1}{2}\left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right). \ee

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic expansion of connections satisfying the field equations
nodes.statement: Thus, the asymptotically hyperbolic connections satisfying field equations take the form \be A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}\Big(e_{(0)}^i+\rho \omega_{(0)}^i+\frac{\rho^2}{2} \left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j+\rho^3 e_{(3)}^i+\cdots\Big). \ee This differs from the connection (\ref{A-metric}) computed from an asymptotically hyperbolic metric with the absence of a $d\rho$ term. The two connections are nonetheless gauge equivalent. We emphasise that the connection has the expansion as above for any member of our class of gravity theories, including GR.
nodes.statement_short: The connection analogue of the Fefferman--Graham expansion: boundary coframe, boundary Levi-Civita connection, boundary Schouten-type term, then free data at order $\rho^3$ -- universal across all deformed theories.
assumptions: the asymptotically hyperbolic connections satisfying field equations
for any member of our class of gravity theories, including GR
conclusions: $A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}\Big(e_{(0)}^i+\rho \omega_{(0)}^i+\frac{\rho^2}{2} \left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j+\rho^3 e_{(3)}^i+\cdots\Big)$
The two connections are nonetheless gauge equivalent
the connection has the expansion as above for any member of our class of gravity theories, including GR

nodes.name: Free data at order $\rho^3$ and higher-order determinacy
nodes.statement: This expansion is the analog of the metric expansion reviewed in the Introduction. The freedom that arises in the expansion of $m^{ij}$ at order $m_{(3)}^{ij}$ translates into the freedom in $X_{(3)}^{ij}$, which in turn translates into $e_{(3)}^i$ being not completely determined. After the free part of $e_{(3)}^i$ is specified, the connection equations can be solved order by order in the expansion parameter, with no further ambiguity.
nodes.statement_short: The freedom in $m_{(3)}$ propagates to $e_{(3)}$; once that is fixed, all higher orders are determined.

nodes.name: Matrix of curvature wedge products from the solved connection
nodes.statement: It is a useful exercise to compute the matrix $X^{ij}$ of curvature wedge products directly from (\ref{A-final}). We have \begin{multline} F^i\wedge F^j = - 2\frac{d\rho}{\rho^2} \wedge e_{(0)}^{(i} \wedge \frac{1}{2\rho^2} \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge e_{(0)}^l \\ -2\frac{d\rho}{\rho^2} \wedge e_{(0)}^{(i} \wedge ( f^{j)}_{(0)} + \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge(Re_{(0)})^l )\\ + 2d\rho \wedge(R e_{(0)})^{(i} \wedge \frac{1}{2\rho^2} \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge e_{(0)}^l + \ldots, \end{multline} where we denoted \be (Re_{(0)})^i:= \left( R^{ij} - \frac{1}{3} R \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j, \ee and dots stand for terms of order $d\rho/\rho$ and higher. These terms vanish when the trace is taken, and so will not contribute into our computation of the divergent terms below.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $F^i\wedge F^j$ for the solved asymptotically hyperbolic connection, to the orders relevant for the divergences.

nodes.name: Expansion of the auxiliary matrix $M$ in GR
nodes.statement: As we have previously established, this matrix has the following expansion (in the case of GR): \be M = \frac{3}{\Lambda} \left( \id + O(\rho^3) \right), \ee where moreover the order $\rho^3$ term is tracefree.

nodes.name: Divergences of the action are those of the boundary Chern--Simons functional
nodes.statement: We now combine (\ref{X-soln}) and (\ref{M-soln}) to compute the divergent contributions. The leading term in (\ref{X-soln}) is a multiple of the identity matrix. Hence, because of the trace free character of the order $\rho^3$ term in (\ref{M-soln}), there is no contribution from that term and this is why it was not necessary to compute it. Thus, all the divergent terms in (\ref{action}) are the same as those in the functional \be \frac{3}{\Lambda}\int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon}[A] , \ee where $S^{CS}$ is the Chern-Simons functional (\ref{CS}). The minus sign in (\ref{bulk-bound}) is due to our choice of the orientation: we have placed the asymptotic boundary in the bulk integral on the lower limit of integration.  We thus see that the boundary term necessary to remove the divergences arising in the bulk integration is just a multiple of the boundary Chern-Simons action. This gives another reason for selecting the Chern-Simons functional of the boundary connection as the boundary term in our action principle: it serves both the purpose of making the variational principle well-defined as well as renormalising the action by subtracting the divergent contributions.
nodes.statement_short: Because $M$ deviates from the identity only at order $\rho^3$ and tracelessly, all divergences of the action equal those of $-\tfrac{3}{\Lambda}S^{CS}$ on the cut-off boundary.
assumptions: The leading term in (\ref{X-soln}) is a multiple of the identity matrix
because of the trace free character of the order $\rho^3$ term in (\ref{M-soln})
conclusions: all the divergent terms in (\ref{action}) are the same as those in the functional $\frac{3}{\Lambda}\int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon}[A]$
the boundary term necessary to remove the divergences arising in the bulk integration is just a multiple of the boundary Chern-Simons action

nodes.name: Explicit divergences of $\int{\rm Tr}(F\wedge F)$
nodes.statement: It is interesting to compute the divergences directly. Taking the trace of (\ref{X-soln}), and using the fact that the matrix in $(Re_{(0)})$ is trace free, we get \be \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = -2 \int_{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} (3 + \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(f)) + \ldots= -\frac{2}{\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 - \frac{2}{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 \,{\rm Tr}(f)+ \ldots, \ee where dots stand for finite parts, and $dv_0$ is the volume form for the metric with triad $e_{(0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The Pontryagin integral diverges as $\epsilon^{-3}$ and $\epsilon^{-1}$ with boundary volume and curvature-trace coefficients.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume in the connection setup
nodes.statement: Finally, we can define the notion of renormalised volume in the connection setup. We define it as \be -2 \Lambda \, RV= \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left( \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) + \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon} \right), \ee where we took (\ref{volume}) into account.
nodes.statement_short: The renormalised volume is the regularised bulk action with a single boundary Chern--Simons counter term.
nodes.definiendum: renormalised volume $RV$ in the connection setup
nodes.genus: limit of the regularised bulk action

nodes.name: Different $1/\epsilon$ coefficient than in the metric setup
nodes.statement: We note that the coefficient in front of $1/\epsilon$ term in our connection setup is different from that in the metric setup, see (\ref{RV}). This is because we are working in a different gauge and the metric as computed from the connection would have had the mixed $d\rho dx^i$ terms. These would change the computation of the renormalised volume above. There would be extra sub-leading terms present that would change the coefficient in front of the $1/\epsilon$ term.
nodes.statement_short: The subleading counter-term coefficient differs from the metric computation because a different gauge is used.

nodes.name: Shift of the Chern--Simons functional under large gauge transformations
nodes.statement: It remains invariant under small gauge transformations (homotopic to the identity). Under the so-called large gauge transformations, Chern--Simons functional changes (in our normalisation) by an integral multiple of $8\pi^2$, so that $S^{CS}/4\pi$ changes by a multiple of $2\pi$. More precisely, there is a natural isomorphism $H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$; now given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle, write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong \Z$, then $S^{CS}(g^*(A)) = 8\pi^2 n + S^{CS}(A)$.
nodes.statement_short: $S^{CS}$ is invariant under small gauge transformations and shifts by $8\pi^2 n$, $n=g_*[X]\in H_3({\rm SU}(2))$, under large ones.
assumptions: given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle
write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong \Z$
conclusions: It remains invariant under small gauge transformations (homotopic to the identity)

nodes.name: Renormalised volume defined modulo a constant
nodes.statement: Thus, our renormalised volume is defined modulo addition of a constant: \be RV\in \mathbb{R}\quad {\rm mod} \quad \frac{3}{2\Lambda^2} 8\pi^2. \ee
assumptions: our renormalised volume is defined using a multiple of the Chern--Simons functional for the renormalisation
Chern--Simons functional changes (in our normalisation) by an integral multiple of $8\pi^2$
conclusions: $RV\in \mathbb{R}\quad {\rm mod} \quad \frac{3}{2\Lambda^2} 8\pi^2$

nodes.name: Einstein--Hilbert action on shell as a multiple of the volume
nodes.statement: This has interesting consequences. The Riemannian signature Einstein--Hilbert action \be S_{\rm EH} = -\frac{1}{16\pi G} \int \sqrt{g} (R-2\Lambda) \ee becomes, on Einstein metrics $R_{\mu\nu}=\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, a multiple of the total volume of the space \be S = -\frac{\Lambda}{8\pi G} V. \ee

nodes.name: Path integral over asymptotically hyperbolic connections
nodes.statement: In the connection setup, we want to do a path integral over connections \be \int {\cal D}A \, \exp{\frac{i}{\hbar} S[A]}. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Make the connection-space path integral $\int\mathcal DA\,e^{iS[A]/\hbar}$ well defined.

nodes.name: Connection action defined modulo a constant
nodes.statement: This means that in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting, our connection action is again only defined modulo a constant: \be S  \in \mathbb{R} \quad {\rm (mod)} \quad \frac{3}{8 G \Lambda} 2\pi. \ee
assumptions: in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting we need to add a multiple of the Chern--Simons functional of the boundary connection to our bulk action
conclusions: our connection action is again only defined modulo a constant
$S  \in \mathbb{R} \quad {\rm (mod)} \quad \frac{3}{8 G \Lambda} 2\pi$

nodes.name: Quantisation of the Hubble length in Planck units
nodes.statement: If we want the path integral to be insensitive to this ambiguity we should require that the phase in $\exp{i S/\hbar}$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$. This gives the following quantisation condition \be \frac{1}{8 G \hbar} = \frac{N\Lambda}{3}, \qquad N\in {\mathbb N}. \ee To put it differently, introducing the Planck length $l_P^2 = G\hbar$ and the Hubble length $\Lambda/3=1/L^2$ we get \be L^2 = 8 N l_P^2, \ee the Hubble length is quantised in units of the Planck length.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness of the path integral forces $L^2=8Nl_P^2$: the cosmological constant is quantised in Planck units.
assumptions: If we want the path integral to be insensitive to this ambiguity we should require that the phase in $\exp{i S/\hbar}$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$
conclusions: $\frac{1}{8 G \hbar} = \frac{N\Lambda}{3}, \qquad N\in {\mathbb N}$
the Hubble length is quantised in units of the Planck length

nodes.name: Relation to the cosmological constant problem
nodes.statement: Of course, we have derived the above quantisation condition working with asymptotically hyperbolic connections corresponding to negative scalar curvature. Observations indicate that our Universe is filled with dark energy whose equation of state is consistent with having a {\it positive} cosmological constant. If we extrapolate (\ref{quant}) to the setting of positive $\Lambda$, then, for all quantities as observed $N$ is very large $8N = L^2/l_P^2 \sim 10^{120}$, and is the number embodying the famous cosmological constant problem.
nodes.statement_short: Extrapolated to positive $\Lambda$, the integer $N$ is of order $10^{120}$ -- the cosmological constant problem.

nodes.name: Two metric counter terms combine into a single Chern--Simons term
nodes.statement: One of the most interesting features of the connection setting is that the two different counter terms that are required in the metric setup in the process of evaluation of the renormalised volume combine into a single Chern--Simons term. This can be seen with almost no computation, and results from the fact that the auxiliary matrix $M$ that appears in the Lagrangian has the expansion that starts with sufficiently high order so that the divergences of the volume are exactly those of the integral $\int {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F)$ of the Pontryagin density. The latter is a boundary term given by the Chern--Simons functional of the connection. An example of the computation of renormalised volume in the language of connections, together with analysis of the behaviour under the deformation of the theory, will appear as a separate publication.
nodes.statement_short: The high order at which $M$ departs from the identity is what merges both metric counter terms into one Chern--Simons boundary term.

nodes.name: Analogy with three-dimensional Riemannian gravity
nodes.statement: It should also be said that the quantisation condition (\ref{quant}) is reminiscent of what happens in the setting of Riemannian signature gravity in three dimensions (with positive $\Lambda$), where the full action, not just the boundary term as here, is given by the Chern-Simons functional of a certain ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection. Similar large gauge transformation considerations show that the cosmological constant must be quantised in this setting, see e.g., \cite{Freidel:1998ua} where this fact is reviewed.
nodes.statement_short: The same large-gauge argument quantises $\Lambda$ in 3D Riemannian gravity, where the whole action is Chern--Simons.

nodes.name: Comparison with Anderson's Chern--Gauss--Bonnet renormalisation
nodes.statement: We also note that the fact that the Chern--Simons functional renormalises the volume is analogous to the statement in \cite{Anderson} that the boundary term at infinity in the Chern--Gauss--Bonnet formula renormalises the volume. The statement in this paper is similar, except that we use the integral of the first Pontryagin density of the bundle, not the Euler density, for the renormalisation.
nodes.statement_short: Analogous to Anderson's Chern--Gauss--Bonnet renormalisation, but using the Pontryagin rather than the Euler density.

nodes.name: Admissibility of the partial gauge fixing
nodes.statement: We can thus partially gauge fix the diffeomorphism and gauge freedom restricting our considerations to asymptotically hyperbolic connections of the form $$A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$ with $e^i$ symmetric and trace 3 with respect to the frame $e^i_{(0)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Diffeomorphisms plus gauge transformations suffice to bring any asymptotically hyperbolic connection to the form $A^i=e^i/\rho+\omega^i_{(0)}$ with $e^i$ symmetric.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
assumptions: the gauge freedom of diffeomorphisms plus gauge transformations
conclusions: restricting our considerations to asymptotically hyperbolic connections of the form $A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)}$
with $e^i$ symmetric and trace 3 with respect to the frame $e^i_{(0)}$

nodes.name: Recursive construction of the partial gauge fixing
nodes.statement: Under an infinitesimal diffeomorphism generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and infinitesimal gauge transformation generated by $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\su(2))$ the connection (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) transformations as \begin{multline*} \delta_{\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho+\varphi}A^i =\frac{1}{\rho}(\cL^X_\xi e^i_{(0)}+\epsilon^{ijk}e^j_{(0)}\varphi^k-\lambda e^i_{(0)}) \\ +\cL^X_\xi \omega^i_{(0)}+d^X\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\omega_{(0)}^j\varphi^k+\cL^X_\xi a^i+\epsilon^{ijk}a^j\varphi^k+\rho(\lambda \dot a^i+b^id^X\lambda) \\ +\Big(\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)\Big)d\rho \end{multline*} The idea now is to set $b^i$ and the anti-symmetric and trace parts of (the subleading orders of) $\langle a^i,e^j_{(0)}\rangle$ to zero by (infinitesimal) diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations. Indeed, we may impose $$b^i+\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)=0,$$ \begin{multline*} \epsilon^{ijk}\langle a^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{2}{\rho}\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle d^X\varphi^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle \\ +\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle \varphi^i-\langle \omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle \varphi^k+\langle a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^i-\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k \\ +\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL_\xi^Xa^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL^X_{\xi}e^j_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle +\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL^X_{\xi}\omega_{(0)}^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle \\ +\rho(\lambda\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \dot a^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\epsilon^{ijk}b^j\langle d^X\lambda,e^k_{(0)}\rangle)=0, \end{multline*} \begin{multline*} \langle a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\frac{3}{\rho}\lambda+\rho(\lambda\langle \dot a^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+b^k\langle d^X\lambda,e^k_{(0)}\rangle) \\ +\langle\cL_\xi^Xa^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\langle \cL^X_{\xi}e^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle \cL^X_{\xi}\omega_{(0)}^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle \\ +\langle d^X\varphi^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\epsilon^{klm}\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^l_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^m-\epsilon^{klm}\langle a^k,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^m=0, \end{multline*} which can be solved recursively starting with, say, $\xi_{(0)}=0$, $\varphi_{(0)}^i=0$ and $\lambda_{(0)}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the variation of the connection under diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations, impose the gauge conditions, and solve the resulting system recursively order by order.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections

nodes.name: Compute the gauge and diffeomorphism variation of the connection
nodes.statement: Under an infinitesimal diffeomorphism generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and infinitesimal gauge transformation generated by $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\su(2))$ the connection (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) transformations as \begin{multline*} \delta_{\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho+\varphi}A^i =\frac{1}{\rho}(\cL^X_\xi e^i_{(0)}+\epsilon^{ijk}e^j_{(0)}\varphi^k-\lambda e^i_{(0)}) \\ +\cL^X_\xi \omega^i_{(0)}+d^X\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\omega_{(0)}^j\varphi^k+\cL^X_\xi a^i+\epsilon^{ijk}a^j\varphi^k+\rho(\lambda \dot a^i+b^id^X\lambda) \\ +\Big(\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)\Big)d\rho \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Write down the full variation of $A^i$ under $(\xi,\lambda,\varphi)$.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections

nodes.name: Impose the gauge conditions
nodes.statement: The idea now is to set $b^i$ and the anti-symmetric and trace parts of (the subleading orders of) $\langle a^i,e^j_{(0)}\rangle$ to zero by (infinitesimal) diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the gauge parameters so that $b^i$ and the antisymmetric and trace parts of $a^i$ vanish.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections

nodes.name: Solve the gauge conditions recursively
nodes.statement: which can be solved recursively starting with, say, $\xi_{(0)}=0$, $\varphi_{(0)}^i=0$ and $\lambda_{(0)}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the resulting equations order by order starting from trivial zeroth-order data.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections

nodes.name: Residual diffeomorphism, rescaling and gauge freedom
nodes.statement: There still remains some diffeomorphism and gauge freedom: infinitesimal diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\su(2))$ satisfying $$\frac{1}{\rho}\dot \xi^i+\dot \xi^k\langle\omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\dot\varphi^i+\dot \xi^k\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle=0,$$ \begin{multline*} \frac{2}{\rho}(\varphi^i-\varphi_{(0)}^i)+\epsilon^{ijk}\langle d^X(\varphi^j-\varphi_{(0)}^j),e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^i-\varphi_{(0)}^i)-\langle \omega^i_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^k-\varphi_{(0)}^k) \\ +\langle a^k,e^i_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k_{(0)}-\langle a^i,e^k_{(0)}\rangle\varphi^k+2\langle d^X\lambda_{(0)},e^i_{(0)}\rangle \\ +\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL_\xi^Xa^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}e^j_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle +\epsilon^{ijk}\langle \cL^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}\omega_{(0)}^j,e^k_{(0)}\rangle -\epsilon^{ijk}\langle a^j,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\langle \cL^X_{\xi_{(0)}} e^l_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle=0, \end{multline*} \begin{multline*} -\frac{3}{\rho}(\lambda-\lambda_{(0)}) +\langle\cL_\xi^Xa^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\frac{1}{\rho}\langle \cL^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}e^k_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle+\langle \cL^X_{\xi-\xi_{(0)}}\omega_{(0)}^k,e^k_{(0)}\rangle -\langle a^k,e^l_{(0)}\rangle\langle \cL^X_{\xi_{(0)}} e^l_{(0)},e^k_{(0)}\rangle \\ +\langle d^X(\varphi^k-\varphi_{(0)}^k),e^k_{(0)}\rangle-\epsilon^{klm}\langle \omega^k_{(0)},e^l_{(0)}\rangle(\varphi^m-\varphi_{(0)}^m)=0, \end{multline*} for arbitrary $\xi_{(0)}\in\Gamma(TX)$,$\lambda_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X)$ and $\varphi^i_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X,\su(2))$, do not alter the form of the connection. These equations can again be solved recursively leading to a residual boundary diffeomorphism, rescaling and gauge freedom.
nodes.statement_short: After the partial gauge fixing there remains a residual boundary diffeomorphism, conformal rescaling and gauge freedom.
nodes.section: Partial gauge fixing of asymptotically hyperbolic connections
assumptions: infinitesimal diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\su(2))$ satisfying
for arbitrary $\xi_{(0)}\in\Gamma(TX)$,$\lambda_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X)$ and $\varphi^i_{(0)}\in C^\infty(X,\su(2))$
conclusions: do not alter the form of the connection
These equations can again be solved recursively leading to a residual boundary diffeomorphism, rescaling and gauge freedom

nodes.name: 3+1 form of the Lagrangian
nodes.statement: The Lagrangian \eqref{action} thus take the following 3+1 form \be S[A,M,\mu] = \int_M \left( M^{ij} f_\alpha^{i} \wedge \left(  \dot\alpha^{j}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j}\right) - \mu \, g(M) \right) \W d\rho. \ee where we implemented the constraint with a 3-form Lagrange multiplier $\mu \in \Lambda^3\left(X \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: The action rewritten in 3+1 form with a 3-form Lagrange multiplier enforcing $g(M)=0$.
nodes.section: Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Momenta of the 3+1 Lagrangian
nodes.statement: The associated momenta are: \begin{align*} \pi^i := \pi^i_{\alpha} = M^{ij} f^i_\alpha \;; & & \pi^i_{\beta}=0 \;; & & \pi^{ij}_M =0 \;; & & \pi_{\mu}=0. \end{align*} Note that $\dot{\alpha}$ do not appear in the right-hand-side of the first equation, thus we cannot invert the system and write $\pi_{\alpha}$ as a function of $\dot{\alpha}$. The same is true for all other momenta. This means that we have to keep track of the above equations as constraints on the phase space.
nodes.statement_short: All momenta are constrained: none can be inverted for the velocities, so they are primary constraints.
nodes.section: Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Generalised Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: The generalised Hamiltonian associated to the Lagrangian has all these constraints added with corresponding Lagrange multipliers \begin{multline} H[\alpha, \pi, \beta, \pi_{\beta}, M , \pi_M ,u,v,w] = \int_X -\beta^{i}\left( d^X_\alpha\pi^i \right)  + \mu \, g(M) \\ + u^i \W  \left(\pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha\right) + v^i \W \pi^i_{\beta} + w^{ij} \W \pi^{ij}_M + x \pi_{\mu} \end{multline} where $u$, $v$, $w$ and $x$ are Lagrange multipliers introduced to take care of the constraints on the momenta. We also used integration by parts to make explicit the role of $\beta^i$ as a Lagrange multiplier.
nodes.statement_short: The total Hamiltonian with all primary constraints adjoined by Lagrange multipliers $u,v,w,x$.
nodes.section: Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
differentia: has all these constraints added with corresponding Lagrange multipliers
$u$, $v$, $w$ and $x$ are Lagrange multipliers introduced to take care of the constraints on the momenta

nodes.name: Secondary constraints and Hamilton's equations
nodes.statement: We have the secondary constraints: \begin{align*} \dot{\pi}_{\beta}=0& \Leftrightarrow d^X_{\alpha} \pi^i =0 \\ \dot{\pi}_{M} =0& \Leftrightarrow  \mu \frac{\pa g}{\pa M^{ij}} = u^{(i} \W f^{j)}_{\alpha} \\ \dot{\pi}_{\mu}=0& \Leftrightarrow g\left(M \right)=0 \end{align*} At this point, Hamilton's equations read: \begin{align*} &\dot{\pi}^i = -[\beta,\pi]^i + d^X_{\alpha} \left( M^{ij} u^j\right) \;;& & \dot{\alpha}^i = d^X_{\alpha} \beta^i + u^i. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The secondary constraints reproduce the Gauss constraint, the $M$ equation and $g(M)=0$; Hamilton's equations give the evolution of $\pi^i$ and $\alpha^i$.
nodes.section: Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations

nodes.name: Hamiltonian formulation reproduces the field equations
nodes.statement: We can now solve for $u^i$ and obtain the first equation in (\ref{feqs}). The second secondary constraint becomes \begin{align} \mu \frac{\pa g}{\pa M^{ij}} = X^{ij} \end{align} Altogether, we have reproduced the complete equations of the theory from the Hamiltonian viewpoint.
nodes.statement_short: Eliminating $u^i$ recovers the evolution equation and the $M$ equation, so the Hamiltonian analysis reproduces the full field equations.
nodes.section: Hamiltonian formulation of the connection field equations
assumptions: We can now solve for $u^i$
conclusions: obtain the first equation in (\ref{feqs})
$\mu \frac{\pa g}{\pa M^{ij}} = X^{ij}$
we have reproduced the complete equations of the theory from the Hamiltonian viewpoint

nodes.name: Tertiary constraints not analysed
nodes.statement: In principle, we should also take care of the secondary constraint $\left\{ H , \pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha \right\}=0$ together with tertiary constraints possibly arising. We do not carry out this analysis here as it is not necessary to obtain the field equations. We also note that one way to complete the Hamiltonian analysis is via an Ashtekar-like Hamiltonian formulation, which for modified theories considered here was described in \cite{Krasnov:2008zz}.
nodes.statement_short: The full constraint algebra is left unanalysed; an Ashtekar-like formulation would complete it.
